title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
venue: CHI ’26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school students want an AI system to participate in collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS). The authors note that most prior educational GenAI work frames AI as a tutor or coach for individual learners, while much less is known about AI as a peer collaborator in small-group math work. The study asks how students perceive AI peer support during CPS and what behaviors, features, and controls they want from such a system.

To study this, the researchers ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students in the United States. Students first completed human-only mathematics CPS tasks and then interacted with two AI peers in a technology-probe sandbox built around grade-aligned middle school math problems. They also reviewed AI dialogue excerpts, co-designed ideal AI peer behaviors and personas, completed surveys about preferred AI peer features, and participated in interviews and whole-class reflections. The study used paired quantitative comparisons of human-only versus AI-peer-supported CPS on self-report measures of workload and group climate, alongside qualitative thematic analysis of interviews, reflections, and design artifacts.

Findings show that students preferred AI peers that give hints, checks, and concept refreshers before direct answers, and that keep control in the students’ hands. They wanted the AI to be competent but deferential, to use a friendly peer-like tone, and to support collaboration without being overly “teachery” or taking over the work. Compared with human-only CPS, the AI peer condition reduced perceived time pressure but increased physical effort and reduced some aspects of group cohesion. The paper concludes that students value an AI peer that scaffolds collaboration while preserving co-agency, social attunement, and emotional support, and it offers design recommendations for future AI systems in middle school math teamwork.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/participatory design study with some paired quantitative comparisons, but it is not a controlled intervention trial designed to estimate learning effects. The methodology is clear and systematic, yet the evidence is mainly exploratory and user-experience oriented rather than efficacy-focused.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows large effects on workload and group-process perceptions, but these are not direct learning gains and arise from a prototype AI peer in a short camp context. Its practical impact is promising for design, but the educational outcome evidence is indirect and not yet generalizable.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4o-backed AI peer technology probe for middle school collaborative mathematics problem solving, framed as two student-like AI teammates that provide stepwise discussion, hints, checks, and peer-style dialogue during group work.

finding.finding_summary: In a participatory design study with 24 middle school students (n=24; paired survey analyses n=22), the AI peer condition changed collaboration quality in both positive and negative ways. Students reported significantly lower temporal workload on NASA-TLX (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs. 9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002, d=1.15) but also lower group social attraction (ATGS: M=5.21, SD=1.81 vs. 6.50, SD=2.05; p=0.029, d=0.94) and lower task integration/coordination (GIT: M=4.76, SD=1.58 vs. 5.54, SD=1.52; p=0.047, d=0.81) than human-only CPS. Qualitative data from 18 interviews and 5 whole-class reflection sessions showed students wanted co-agency, responsiveness, and peer-like turn-taking rather than didactic control.
finding.measure: GEQ (Attractions to Group-Social, Group Integration-Task), NASA-TLX workload dimensions, interviews/reflections about collaboration
finding.study_size: n=22 (paired quantitative analyses); n=24 enrolled; n=18 interviews

finding.finding_summary: The AI peer condition reduced perceived time pressure during collaborative math problem solving, indicating improved procedural efficiency. On NASA-TLX temporal demand, students reported substantially lower scores with AI peers (M=5.67, SD=4.38) than in pure human CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13), with a large paired effect (p=0.002, d=1.15; n=22 paired participants). However, the same condition increased physical demand (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs. 4.90, SD=2.41; p=0.014, d=1.14), reflecting added interaction overhead from the text-based interface.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand
